rv.q: It is, quite simply, the most entertaining homegrown play I’ve seen since Till the Stars Come Down, Beth Steel’s wedding day masterpiece at the National.
Wynter has written something wise, witty and packed with big feelings.
What is an unending delight is the frank, witty and expletive-filled conversation between Tillie and her sisters Jackie (Jodie McNee) and heavily pregnant Ann (Charlotte Jaconelli).
Zinging dialogue and bouncing one-liners give wings to a fairly predictable rites-of-passage plot and to characters who begin by looking one-dimensional.
It teems with vulgar wit and life, and Tim Sheader’s production features a host of fine performances.
ILFORD Boy is a colourful rites-of-passage story by actor-writer Danny Lee Wynter about growing up as a gay teenager in 1980s and 90s Essex.
It honours both family and found family, cherishes the bravery of ordinary people in the face of adversity and prejudice, celebrates acceptance and is written with huge heart and wit.
Gossamer-light and sequin-sparkly, this bittersweet new play by Danny Lee Wynter is as beguiling as it is insubstantial.
The busy script from the Black Superhero playwright is crammed with a fractious extended family treading heavily over old arguments, but the production sings when an old friend swans back into town.

ILFORD BOY is chatty, nuanced, playful, crass, foul-mouthed and the characters are well-honed and utterly relatable to a modern audience thanks to the sharp writing and Tim Sheader ’s excellent direction.
Wynter champions those who pave the way and offer safety for the next generation.
Danny Lee Wynter 's new work, Ilford Boy is a witty, sensitive and beautifully performed piece of theatre that will warm your soul and break your heart a little.

Wynter himself grew up in east London and presumably pours some of his own experiences into what ultimately unwinds as a by-turns acutely funny and desperately sad tapestry of a very particular time and place.
Wynter’s sharply observational writing makes character the key, with a cast of believable personalities all dealing with their own challenges.
It doesn’t travel quite as far as it might, but it’s a hugely entertaining journey.

What emerges is a tender, often hilarious exploration of grief, love, identity and the complexities of family life.
The neon lights in Peter McKintosh’s two-storey set add a welcome touch of razzle to this lovely, compassionate play.

cn.t: Danny Lee Wynter's semi-autobiographical coming-of-age tale earns warm praise for its heart, humor, and performances, though critics find the sprawling family drama somewhat unfocused and sitcom-like in structure.
